subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speechtext: Mr. David A. Croll (Spadina) presented the first report of the special committee on defence expenditure, and moved that the report be concurred in.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Before the motion is carried I have just a word to say. If we revert to times gone by, in Hansard of July 3, 1935, at page 4198 there appears the following discussion:

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: -the comptroller of the treasury's office is no good and I protest against this vote-

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: -the comptroller of the treasury took over certain of the functions which formerly belonged to the Auditor General.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, several of the departmental functions in connection with disbursements.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: The expenditures in that one branch are getting to be very large.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It has control over all the disbursements of the country.
Mortuus adhuc loquitur!
Well, sir, I want to bring to the attention of members of the committee the fact that since Mr. Bennett, not by legislation but by order in council, changed the auditing system of all departments by centralizing them under the comptroller of the treasury, no minister except the Minister of Finance is responsible for any expenditures in any department.
It was not Liberal policy, it was Tory policy, and I opposed it bitterly at the time.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order. The motion before the house is to concur in the first report of the special committee on defence expenditure. The committee report is a recommendation to the house that the committee be empowered to print from day to day 750 copies in English and 200 copies in French of the minutes of proceedings and evidence, etc., and to sit while the house is sitting. I do not believe such a' recommendation would permit a general discussion of the matters which have been referred to the committee or a discussion of the procedure in the committee.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you permit me, what I said was the preamble of the
argument that I am going to make now. It will be very short and to the point.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Tell us what you have been doing for the last seventeen years if you objected to that policy.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: I will tell the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) that this was one of the most onerous legacies that a subsequent government inherited from the late Mr. Bennett. I know it hurts the Tories, but I am going to make my point. What I am saying is strictly in order, as you will see, Mr. Speaker, and as hon. members will see. I am not a miracle man. I cannot make the blind see, nor can I make the deaf hear. I know that it hurts, and I am sorry. I do not say this to hurt anyone; I say it to tell the truth and to guard against any injustice being done to either one of the Ministers of National Defence.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member
now to discuss the motion. The motion is that the committee be empowered to print from day to day 750 copies in English and 200 copies in French of its minutes of proceedings and evidence, and such papers and records as may be ordered by the committee to be printed, and that standing order 64 be suspended in relation thereto; (2) to sit while the house is sitting. It is only those two matters which can be discussed at this time.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is more to it.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order, order.

I want the evidence to be
taken by the committee to be in accordance with the elementary rules of justice, and I do not want the committee to sit while the house is sitting to commit any injustice with regard to anyone. It is for this reason, sir, that I bring to the attention of the hon. gentlemen, especially those who will serve on the committee, the fact that hundreds of accountants in the Department of National Defence are not under the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). They are under the comptroller of the treasury since Mr. Bennett centralized the whole business of government payments.

subtopic: CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext: That on Monday, February 2, and on Wednesday, February 4, 1953, and every Monday and Wednesday thereafter to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.

maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
I do not
propose to debate this motion, but it occurs to me to wonder whether the Prime Minister has given any consideration to the suggestion that, instead of taking away both Mondays and Wednesdays at this stage, he might devote the Mondays to government business and leave the Wednesdays for a period of another two or three weeks. At this stage of the session, Wednesday is only a half day and there are a lot of private members' motions remaining on the order paper. Speaking as one who has been fortunate enough to have his motion called, I can say that I know there are others who have not had such good fortune. I am sure these members would appreciate it if Wednesday could be left for the time being.

maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
It has been the practice
in some of the former sessions to take away the Mondays first and then afterwards the Wednesdays, but that has always been when the Mondays were being taken very much earlier than has been the case this session. There have been more days allotted to the application of the ordinary rules this session than for a very long time hitherto. I think there has been an ample opportunity for the discussion of all those notices of motions that members really wish to have discussed. There are two hours remaining when the public bills and orders can be reached if private bills do not occupy all the time allotted. So far private bills have taken up very little of those two hours, so I would imagine there would be no serious inconvenience in proceeding now to the extent which is being proposed.
Prior to Thursday, very little inroad has been made on the long list of government business that has been on the order paper since the opening of the session. We do not like to be arbitrary, but it was felt at this time it was not being arbitrary to propose this motion.

maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
I think it is fair, on this motion, to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a question. It will be recalled that last July when the

question of the adjournment of the 1952 session of parliament until the autumn, and the commencement of the 1953 session in the autumn of 1952, was proposed by the government, I asked him as to the reason for it. The Prime Minister indicated that the purpose of calling parliament so early was to conclude the session at the end of April or the first of May so that those who would be going to the coronation would have an opportunity of doing so. May I ask if that is still the aim of the government with respect to the present session.

maintopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON MONDAYS AND WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
The government still
hopes that will be possible.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue) moved:
speechtext:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development, with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members: Messrs. Beaudry, Boisvert, Breton, Carter, Courte-manche, Decore, Diefenbaker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Fulton, Gauthier (Portneuf), Gauthier (Sudbury), Hansell, Henry, Jones, Kirk (Digby-Yarmouth), Knight, MacLean (Queens), McCann, Murray (Cariboo), Mutch, Richard (Ottawa East), Riley, Robinson, Smith (Moose Mountain), and Whitman. That standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, we have again proposed the appointment of a special committee on radio broadcasting. Regarding the study of all the aspects of the national system the terms of reference are practically the same as those similar committees have had in former years. There is, however, one change in the wording of the notice of motion. As bon. members will note, the resolution reads:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider-
-and so on. Formerly, the word "radio" was inserted in front of the word "broadcasting". It was our former conception in years gone by that broadcasting consisted solely of sound broadcasting or what is known as radio. Within the last few years, however, there has been in this country a new development in the matter of television, so that when we put in the word "broadcasting" without

the word "radio" in front of it, that procedure naturally broadens the scope of the investigation or inquiry that will come before the committee; and it is proposed that they examine into the matters pertaining both to sound broadcasting and to television.
The last committee that sat on this particular subject was in the fall session of 1951. There had previously been an examination in 1950. The committee in 1951 brought in its report. Its sessions were not perhaps as long as usual because of the fact that at that time-in the summer of 1950 and from then on-there had been sitting a commission which had been set up on the development of the arts, letters and sciences and which was commonly known as the Massey commission. That commission had its report ready about that time, and the committee on radio broadcasting made a thorough examination of all the recommendations which were made in that report. The committee itself brought in its report on Friday, December 14, 1951. While it is not my purpose at this time to review extensively the recommendations and the findings of that committee I might, however, bring to your attention some of the recommendations which were made. One in particular was recommendation No. 8 which is as follows:
Your committee shares the view of the royal commission and of the previous committees of the house that the national broadcasting service carried on by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is essential in the development of our national life in Canada, and is efficiently performing an extremely valuable and important function. It has been impressed by the variety and extent of the services being provided by the corporation, and by the complexity of the problems which Canadian conditions impose.
Then the report went on and dealt with the other recommendations, one of which was:
It also recommends the initiation as funds become available of a second French network corresponding to the English language dominion network, the establishment of a French network station in the maritime provinces and increased service of French network programs by transcription to French language stations in the prairie provinces.
The committee recommended the desirability of improving the program services. They made recommendations with reference to the financing of the corporation. They were favourably impressed by the activities of the international services, and in the consideration of the representation of the Canadian Association of Broadcasters they made certain observations. There then came up another important question and their recommendation was this:
That the grant of the privilege of radio broadcasting in Canada continue to be under the control of the national government; that the control
Committee on Broadcasting of the national broadcasting system continue to be vested in a single body responsible to parliament; that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as now constituted be that authority and continue to provide directly by its operations and indirectly by its control of the operations of others a national broadcasting service free from partisan influence.
I am merely bringing these matters to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and I think perhaps the most important one, in the light of developments since 1951, was their recommendation with reference to television. That recommendation was No. 23 in the report and it was as follows:
Your committee is strongly impressed with the vital need for the development of a television system that is essentially Canadian and which gives expression in this new form of broadcasting to Canadian ideas and aspirations. It agrees with the royal commission that the situation must be avoided under which commercial pressures will lead to the major part of the material on Canadian channels being non-Canadian. Your committee supports the recommendations of the royal commission regarding television development and your committee recommends that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proceed as soon as practicable with the extension of television coverage.
What I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, is the fact, that as a result of this investigation by the radio committee in 1951, considerable progress has been made with reference to the implementation of their recommendations. For instance, we have now established a French network in western Canada and also preparations have been made and work is now being done in connection with the French language station down in the maritimes. In addition to that, a number of low-power relay transmitters, as they are called, have been installed in northern Ontario and in northwestern Canada as well as in northwestern Quebec, in order that coverage may be added in those particular regions.
That committee made it a point to visit our facilities in the city of Montreal at the Radio Canada building there, and I am sure they were impressed with the advancements which were being made in the development of that centre.	I would suggest to the
committee this year, when they meet, that they again avail themselves of the opportunity of visiting Montreal or Toronto or perhaps both, and seeing the advancement that has been made there both in the physical attainments and in the technological advancements there have been both in sound broadcasting and in television. You will remember also, Mr. Speaker, that in our discussions in 1951 there was reference to certain amendments to the Canadian Broadcasting Act. At the time when we had the debate on the setting up of the committee we joined together both the resolution with

Committee on Broadcasting reference to the amendments to the broadcasting act and the resolution setting up the committee. May I recall to your memory just what those changes were in the broadcasting act. Two more governors were added to the board of governors which formerly consisted of nine; the board of governors since that time has had a membership of eleven.
Newfoundland, having come into confederation, was entitled to a representative on the board. That member has been appointed and has been functioning on the board ever since.
The second thing that we did under the amendment to the act at that time was to give the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation greater borrowing powers without having reference to the cabinet. Their borrowing powers were increased from $10,000 to $25,000 on any one project. The tenure of office of the chairman was changed. Then we set up an appeal section. We also made it possible by the changes for the chairman of the board, who was appointed by the government and who was not considered as an employee for pension purposes, to be considered as an employee, and he is eligible for pension.
I do not need to say very much more with reference to that, except to point out, as hon. members know, that the C.B.C., being a crown corporation, is probably subject to a great deal of criticism from all parts of the country and from all types of bodies. But still the C.B.C. has a great number of friends. I do not know of any other public institution which receives resolutions from as large a number of influential bodies as does the C.B.C. The federation of agriculture, which is one of the biggest organizations in the whole of the country, as well as the Trades and Labour Congress, different labour bodies, women's institutes and a great many others send in resolutions commending the policies of the C.B.C. I admit that perhaps we do not get the support of wealthy and powerful newspapers and chambers of commerce. While we are not entirely indifferent to them, I think that the other bodies which do pass resolutions commending the work of the C.B.C. are a good deal more influential. In addition to that, they do represent a greater body of public opinion. Of course the C.B.C. has difficulties. Any organization that undertakes a large amount of work in this country, as does the C.B.C., is bound to have difficulties and criticism.
When we are discussing the C.B.C. we should keep in mind that they have to operate on five time zones from one end of the country to the other. They have to

operate in two languages; they have to set up different systems and different networks in order to meet the needs of this country. In addition to the trans-Canada network and the dominion network, it is necessary also to have a French network.
I might recall to hon. members the fact that the C.B.C. has been the subject of investigation ever since its inception. There was the Aird report of years ago, which still is good reading, with reference to the basic principles on which the C.B.C. was founded. From year to year there has been a periodic examination by the radio committee of the House of Commons, and then in 1950 the commission to which I have made reference was set up, namely, the commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. Its report has become known as the Massey report. The government has followed, and intends to follow, fairly exactly I would say, the recommendations that have been made in that report, because there was *never in this country a more extensive and exhaustive report made with reference to broadcasting than was made by the Massey commission. What we asked them to do, and what we are following, was to lay down principles upon which the government could formulate its policy with reference to the C.B.C. I want it distinctly understood that in the matter of internal management there is absolutely no interference on behalf of the government. When it comes to a matter of large expenditure, under the act these things are referred to the government for either endorsation or rejection.
I have always been in favour of private enterprise. Perhaps some people will wonder why I advocate and support the C.B.C. Well, I do it for this reason, that radio broadcasting and television are a natural monopoly. There are only a certain number of frequencies with reference to sound broadcasting, and what we call channels with reference to television, that are available, and if there were not control over them, and some governing body to do the controlling, the whole matter of broadcasting, either sound or television, would soon be chaotic. And so it is when you have a natural monopoly of this kind, it is in the best interests of the great majority of the people of Canada that there should be a governing body so to regulate things that they accrue to the best interests of the greatest number of people.
That is about all I have to say with reference to sound broadcasting. Hon. members will recall that on December 8 I made a statement in this house with reference to government policy on television.

That statement can be found in Hansard of that date at page 409. It was the first item of business of that day. I am not going to read it again; I am going to point out some of the important features in order to refresh our memories when we get into the discussion on television. I said at that time: -the government has been giving careful consideration to the development of television broadcasting in Canada. In its consideration it has had in mind the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences. The commission recommended that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proceed with the production of television programs and with plans for national coverage. It spoke of extension of national coverage both through publicly and privately-owned stations. It said that no private station should be licensed until the C.B.C. had available national television programs and that all private stations established should be required to serve as outlets for national programs. It emphasized the need for direction and control of television broadcasting in Canada to prevent Canadian stations from becoming mere channels for broadcasting material from outside Canada and to encourage Canadian content.
The government believes, with the royal commission, that television should be developed in Canada with the aim of benefiting our national life and that it should have the structure and the means required by Canadian conditions to ensure an adequate amount of suitable Canadian programs for Canadians as well as using some material from outside the country. Television will undoubtedly play a considerable part in the lives of many Canadian families. It is bound to have a strong effect on the growing minds of young people watching it in their own homes. The government believes it should be so developed in Canada that it is capable of providing a sensible pattern of programming for Canadian homes with at least a good portion of Canadian content.
We said at that time:
Therefore, it is proposed to ask parliament to approve a loan to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for the purpose of building stations on the Pacific coast, in the prairie provinces, and in the Atlantic provinces. These would be established in the Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax areas. Thus, in addition to the stations at Montreal and Toronto, and that to be built at Ottawa, there would be publicly-owned stations with some production facilities at least in each of the main regions of the country.
We announced at that time that the government would be in a position to receive applications for licences for private stations to serve areas not now served-and this is very important-to serve areas not now served or to be served by publicly-owned facilities already announced. The government then, at that time, indicated to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that it was prepared to consider applications for such licences as may be recommended by the corporation, after having cleared, of course, with the Department of Transport. At that time I said:
The objective will be to make national television service available to as many Canadians as possible through co-operation between private and public
Committee on Broadcasting enterprise. Under this plan the private stations licensed will carry national program service, besides having time for programming of their own. There will be plenty of opportunity for enterprise by private interests in television broadcasting, and at the same time provision for wide extension of the national service. Since the objective will be to extend services as widely throughout Canada as is practicable, no two stations will be licensed at the present to serve the same area. A television station can serve only a comparatively small area. Canada is very large and it will require a good many stations before television can be brought to the people in most parts of our country.
That works both ways, of course.
Would the minister permit a question arising out of the statement he has just made?

Perhaps the hon. member
would permit me to complete this part of my observations. That works both ways. If the C.B.C. sets up a television station in, we will say, the city of Toronto, and will not allow a licence there for a private station at the same time, that, of course, gives protection to the C.B.C. But if a licence were given in the city of Kitchener, serving a community of perhaps half a million people, a similar protection would be given in that no other licence would be given in that area at this time.
So that, as I say, in my judgment it works both ways, in that it protects the C.B.C. on the one hand and the private stations on the other. I have mentioned Kitchener. The C.B.C. has not designated that as an area to be served by them, so that it will be one available for private stations.

From the last few words of the minister's observations it would appear that the Kitchener area is not one designated as an area to be served by the C.B.C. The question I wish to ask is this:	In view of
the fact that that designation covers not only stations now being erected or shortly to be erected, but also those to be erected in the future, what about the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta? Has it yet been decided whether they are to be C.B.C. areas, or whether private enterprise may enter in those provinces.

In Manitoba we propose to
erect a C.B.C. station in the city of Winnipeg, as has already been announced. Determination has not been made, for instance, with respect to Alberta. But, supposing we did erect a station in Alberta, I presume it would be, perhaps, in the city of Calgary. That leaves a splendid area in the Edmonton community for private broadcasters. They could serve that large area through some origination of programs and by programs

Committee on Broadcasting which are prepared by the C.B.C. and offered to them by means of kinescope recordings. It would serve also as an outlet for C.B.C. programs in the event that technological advances make it possible to bring those programs to that particular city either by means of microwave relay, or by cable.
What about Saskatchewan and British Columbia?

We might hope that probably Saskatchewan could be supplied with programs, on the one side from Manitoba or on the other from Calgary, if there are certain advances made. If not, we would have to give consideration to the establishment of a C.B.C. transmitter in the province of Saskatchewan.
However, those are matters under consideration. I might point out that television is terribly expensive, and it will be hard to get public opinion to support a development at this time to the extent that we would wish. My own policy would be, so far as any advice that I might give is concerned, that we have got to go slowly on this, and take advantage of such technological advances as come along.
Does that not mean that Saskatchewan would be a no-man's-land?
No, you cannot put it that way. Saskatchewan has never been neglected, so far as this government is concerned.

What about British
Columbia?
I have made the announcement that we are building-we have already acquired the land-a television station in the city of Vancouver.
To be built when?
To be built just as soon as plans can be drawn for it, and the transmitter can be supplied.
No, not 1970. We believe that by the end of 1953, or perhaps before that-in the early fall-we will be operating in the city of Vancouver.
Would the minister permit a question?
Would the hon. member let me finish my statement, first.

On the basis of what the minister has said, it is planned to do something in British Columbia by the end of 1953. Is it right to say that, so far as Saskatchewan and Alberta are concerned, there are no plans for 1953, or the immediate future?

Plans are not yet finalized with respect to Alberta and Saskatchewan. But they have been considered, and as soon as policy is determined with respect to those two provinces in the matter of the erection of television stations, it will be announced.
What is the situation in New Brunswick?

Mr. Speaker, I should prefer to have the questions after I have finished what I have to say. I can quite understand that hon. members are inquisitive; and sometimes, too, they may feel that if they can break up what one has to say it will be to their own advantage. I am just as familiar with those tricks as is the hon. member for Lake Centre. However, under the circumstances I think we will just let that go by the board.
I think you had better.

May I now return to the matter about which I wish to speak. I have given the policy of the government regarding the licensing of television stations. I should like now to review briefly the development of television broadcasting in this country, and refer to some facts in connection with it.
As hon. members will recall, television was one of the subjects the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences was asked to study. The government, however, did not wish to delay all action until the commission could make its examination, and report its findings. Therefore at the time the commission was set up the government authorized the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to proceed with plans for production centres and transmitting stations at Montreal and Toronto, as the first steps in the Canadian system.
Loans were authorized to finance these projects. The C.B.C. was able to go ahead, starting in 1950. Shortage of steel and all other materials and equipment following the outbreak of the Korean war held up these projects considerably and, in fact, delayed their completion for about a year. These centres went into regular operation in September of 1952. I, personally, have visited them and have seen the production of programs taking place. I would hope that other members of the House of Commons who are interested in this subject would do the same. It is only by seeing, at first hand, that anyone can grasp the immense effort and the complicated organization that is necessary to produce a live program. Early in 1951, in the light of the steel situation, the government decided to stop authorizing any new broadcasting stations for sound or television at a time when steel was being

withheld from so many other purposes. Those restrictions were lifted at the end of December, 1952. In recent months, due to the improvement of the steel situation, the government has given consideration to the question of television development.
I have already said that it was decided to ask parliament for a loan to enable the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to establish further stations at the capital and also one each in the Pacific, prairie and Atlantic regions. We also gave careful consideration to the part which private stations should play in the development. In this connection I should like to remind the house of some of the things which the royal commission said in dealing with television, and I should like to quote from the report where it deals with television at page 301 as follows:
1.	We were given the grave responsibility of making recommendations on the principles upon which the policy of Canada should be based in the field of television, this new and unpredictable force in our society. Our recommendations, however, as well as the evidence we bring forward in support of them, can be short and simple. They follow from the fact that the considerations leading us to recommend the continuation of a national system of radio broadcasting seem to us to dictate much more strongly and urgently a similar system in television. Television, like radio, is akin to a monopoly, but its much more limited channels give added importance to a system of co-ordination and control. Like radio it is a valuable instrument of national unity, of education, and of entertainment; how much more valuable it is difficult to say at present, but it promises to be a more popular as well as a more persuasive medium.
2.	The position of private stations in Canadian television broadcasting requires special consideration. In radio broadcasting Canada has achieved maximum coverage for national programs at minimum cost by using some commercial programs, and by co-ordinating private stations within the national system under the control of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We think the same principles of national control should be applied to television broadcasting but with certain special precautions. It seems apparent that the most difficult problem of television in Canada will be to provide programs in our remote and thinly populated areas; and television advertising will raise difficult questions. Even in radio broadcasting the programs of all private stations are likely to suffer from excessive control by the advertising sponsor. Only to a limited degree can the private station operator determine the character of his own programs. Because of greater capital investment and greater operating costs the unfortunate tendencies of radio broadcasting will be intensified in television. The pressure on uncontrolled private television operators to become mere channels for American commercial material will be almost irresistible. In radio broadcasting, Canadians experimented with a purely commercial system before changing to a national system.
That is away back of the Aird report.
Such an experiment with the more costly and powerful television would be dangerous. Once television were established in commercial north-south channels it would be almost impossible to make the expensive changes necessary to link the country

Committee on Broadcasting by national programs on east-west lines of communication. Canadians will welcome good American programs in television as they now do in radio, but as we have been informed, they do not want them at the cost of a Canadian national system, provided that the C.B.C. can make attractive programs available in the not too distant future. It seems desirable to use appropriate American television programs, and to make suitable agreements with Canadian private stations.
That has been accomplished already.
These arrangements, however, should follow and should depend on the organization of a national system of television production and control.
The recommendations were:
We therefore recommend:
a.	That direction and control of television broadcasting in Canada continue to be vested in the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
b.	That the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation proceed with plans for the production of television programs in French and English and for national coverage by kinescope recordings or by any other practicable means.
c.	That no private television broadcasting stations be licensed until the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has available national television programs and that all private stations be required to serve as outlets for national programs.
The policy of the government is designed to carry out the findings of the commission which we believe are of great importance. I suggest that there is no purpose in having investigations such as the Aird commission, committees of the House of Commons or the Massey commission, unless we are prepared to give the recommendations most serious consideration and, I suggest further, to see that they are implemented. I believe that a commission such as the Massey commission represented the best talent available in this country to examine into all phases of the development of broadcasting in Canada. When we got their recommendations, which, after consideration and examination, appeared to be logical and practical to the government, I submit it would be ill-advised if we did not attempt to follow them and give them implementation.
There will be provision for the production of Canadian programs by the C.B.C. over the national service. The C.B.C., of course, will also be able to bring in some suitable programs from outside Canada, as the commission suggests. Just to bring you up to date: We have already made arrangements with the Bell Telephone Company to use their facilities at a rental of $225,000 a year in what is known as the microwave system whereby programs will be brought from Buffalo to-Toronto and, when it is completed, from Buffalo to Montreal and from Montreal to Toronto.

Hear, hear.

It is the most costly of all taxes to collect. The cost of collecting it runs at about 12-2 per cent. The net yield from the tax is about 87 [DOT] 8 per cent. If we had to face expense at that rate in collecting other taxes, the house would throw up its hands in horror. Nevertheless the collection of this tax goes on. The government continues to impose it. Then the Department of Transport a little over a year ago came up with a new idea. They were going to eliminate the house to house canvass and substitute a staff of fifty full-time people who were going to be responsible for collecting this tax. It is about time that the government followed the only sensible course that could be followed with respect to this nuisance tax, and eliminated it.
I said that to my knowledge a number of silent Liberal members in this house disapprove very strongly the imposition of this nuisance tax. They are not alone in their

Committee on Broadcasting party in that respect because at the meeting of the National Liberal Federation in this city on October 27-I wish the hon. and voluble member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Fournier) had remained here because this is a subject that I wished to bring to his attention-we find that that largely attended meeting passed a resolution, which I quote from the Canadian Press dispatch of October 27, as follows:
Recognizing that the use of radio has become universal in Canada and a necessity of modern life, the advisory council recommends that the government give consideration to the immediate abolition of the radio licence fee.
I do not pretend that that resolution gave any comfort to the Minister of National Revenue, nor do I pretend that it brought any comfort to the heart of the minister when, as we read in the press,- he had a stormy and rough ride before that federation when he sought to justify government policy in continuing to impose this $2.50 nuisance tax and to continue monopolistic conditions with respect to television in Canada.
I was not there at all when that was discussed.

Then the press reports must be wrong. It was the policies which the minister had defended so vigorously elsewhere that came under the condemnation of the Liberal federation, just as they would have if the minister had been present.
There is one other matter that I should like to mention before leaving the subject of sound broadcasting.
It is a good time to be away at a time like that.

It was just as well that the minister was not there.
In the recently issued report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1952, we find him dealing with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at page 53 as follows:
The operating surplus of $3,691,779 from sound broadcasting and the $369,225 deficit from television broadcasting may not be regarded as strictly correct, because
(a)	the $14,813,598 income of the corporation and
(b)	the disbursement of $243,353 for loan interest are related in the statement to sound broadcasting only, although pertaining to both sound broadcasting and television.
The correctness of the corporation's liability under the pension plan for past service of employees, reflected in the books by a final payment of $109,255, has yet to be established.
Included as an expense of the year is a charge of $12,000 for the estimated full cost of a deferred pension in favour of the chairman, in respect of the period November, 1945, to December 31, 1951. It was indicated that the matter was still under review, but as the records now are, doubt must necessarily be entertained as to the power of the corporation


(a)	to absorb the cost without cor. :ribution by the chairman:
(b)	to vary the approved pension plan without the concurrence of the governor in council.
Should it be that the action taken is in conflict with section 3(7) of the act, a situation would result which would be unsatisfactory alike to the corporation and the chairman. The matter is accordingly drawn to the notice of the board of governors.
I am sure that this is the first time that it has come to the attention of the house that the C.B.C. took upon itself the power to vote this substantial sum of money to cover the past due liability of the chairman to the pension fund and to do it apparently on a basis that involved a departure from the pension plan applicable to employees and without contribution on the part of the chairman. I suggest that when the committee is set up it should make it its business to inquire into that comment by the Auditor General.
I wish to come now to the subject of television. The minister has said something this afternoon about the importance of television. I am sure that in the world in which we live there are few influences of greater or more growing importance than television, along with radio broadcasting, in the influence they exert on the minds of the people, and particularly on the minds of the young. It is for that reason that I do not think that the house could spend time to better advantage than in carefully considering policies with respect to television.
A release by the dominion bureau of statistics on November 15, 1952, points out that between September 1949 and July 1952, 106,607 television sets were sold in Canada. I suppose that in the light of those figures it is not unfair to estimate that today in Canada there must be at least 150,000 television receiving sets, and the number is growing daily.
The development of television in Canada is years behind the stage of development attained in the United Kingdom and the United States. The reason is that the government has prevented the development of television in Canada. That is the complete reason. The government did it deliberately. We well know that applications for television channels by private applicants have been pending before the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for at least seven years. During all those years the government refused to entertain the applications. It was the policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, as it was the policy of the government, to prevent anyone entering the field of television.
Dog in the manger.

It was a dog-in-the-manger attitude. They would not do it themselves in

those days, and they would not let anybody else do it. It was sheer paternalism on the part of the corporation which led them to say to those who were quite prepared to take all the risks of investing their capital in the development of television in Canada, "Oh, no, we won't let you do it; we know better than you what is good for you; we won't let you do it because you may lose some money even though you might develop television."
So those precious years have passed, and it is only in recent times that the corporation has begun to develop television on its own account. The government deliberately retarded progress. Then along came the Massey report. The fact that the Massey commission was sitting for a year and a half prior to the writing of its report gave the government another excuse for delaying action.
Then the Massey commission made its report and I should like to make an observation about that report. I am sure that all members of the house have read the report with respect. In times past we have debated some of the recommendations made in that report, and some of us expressed and continue to hold a preference for the views expressed on many matters, including radio broadcasting and television, by Dr. Surveyer in his minority report. We accepted those as being the views of a man who by technical experience was better qualified to make recommendations with respect to the technique and system of broadcasting and television in Canada than the other distinguished members of the royal commission.
I wish also to make a general observation about the Massey report. No matter how much respect we may have for the members of the commission or for the views they express on subjects pertaining to Canadian culture, there is nothing in this royal commission report that is sacrosanct. It seems to be the view of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) that, if he breathes the words "royal commission", debate ceases to have any effect and whatever is found in the majority report of the Massey commission must be accepted as final. Well, Mr. Speaker, I for one am not prepared to accept it as final. I am prepared to approach such recommendations with a measure of respect, but I still reserve the right to consider those recommendations; and in this particular case I very much prefer the recommendations of the minority report by Dr. Arthur Surveyer.
Let us have a word about the cost of television in Canada, the cost of development by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. To date it has had these sums placed at its disposal: First of all, $4J million; then another
Committee on Broadcasting $1J million, in 1950, and another $2 million in 1952, or a total so far of $8 million. In the face of all that we have two stations in Canada giving television service to the people of their communities. The only people who are receiving any service in Canada today from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are people who live in Montreal and its immediate vicinity and in Toronto and its immediate vicinity. Those are the only people who so far have enjoyed any of the benefits the minister has proclaimed this afternoon.
Now, the minister has again trotted out that phrase of his, "natural monopoly", to justify the arid, sterile policy the government has been following with respect to television. I say to him that while sound broadcasting, as I indicated earlier, is far from being a natural monopoly, television broadcasting is very much farther removed from being a natural monopoly because of the effective horizon. Any television station has a very limited effective range. That range is normally about 60 miles and in some cases as far as 80 miles. How can it be said that television is a natural monopoly in Canada? It is absurd on the face of it to suggest that.
Mr; McCann: Because of limited channels.

Limited channels, Mr. Speaker? We have great numbers of channels available for television broadcasting in Canada today, channels which are not being used. There are great numbers of them. The fact of the matter is that one channel does not preclude, as it does in the field of sound broadcasting, the enjoyment of the same channel by other television stations as long as they are removed from the effective horizons of each other. It is utter nonsense, Mr. Speaker, for the minister to suggest that we are restricted by a limitation on the number or use of channels. There are many, many channels available today for television in Canada but it is government policy to deny the present use of those channels. I am sure that United States companies operating along the border are going to feel quite at liberty to set up television stations along the border to serve Canadian communities just over the border, even though those same channels are assigned to Canada, because they are not being used today. There are, I am told, many situations of that kind.
Yes, this continued sterilization by the government of the development of television in Canada is fraught with very grave dangers for the whole future of the development of television in Canada.
Now, sir, I have said something about the government's old excuse for its wretched,
1370	HOUSE OF
Committee on Broadcasting dog-in-the-manger attitude, and I have spoken of the delays in the development of the C.B.C.'s television operations. When it finally made up its mind after the Massey commission wrote its report it did run into some difficulties in procuring equipment due to shortages of steel, but let us remember that those long delays occurred and the corporation was obliged to postpone its estimated date for the commencement of operations in Montreal and Toronto not once but a number of times, and for long periods. When the government is building up rosy hopes in the minds of residents of Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax, I would suggest to the residents of those very estimable cities-
Hear, hear.

-that they be not too quick to infer from these government blandishments that they are going to have television service very soon. Because if their experience is anything like the experience of the other two cities which have that service, they are likely to wait a disappointingly long time for the inauguration of the service.
Now, what of government policy today? After this long period of complete sterilization of the development of television, now the government comes forward with what was dressed up to be a new television policy. Oh, the whole country was agog while waiting Tor the enunciation of the new television policy! How we crowded into the Senate [DOT]chamber last November 20 when the speech .from the throne was read, with great expectations, Mr. Speaker, of hearing the announcement of this great, brave new television policy; and this was the dud we had to listen to:
At the time television broadcasting was started in Toronto and Montreal in September, the Prime Minister announced that parliament would be asked to provide for the establishment of three additional public television stations, one in the maritimes, one on the prairies and one on the Pacific coast and that active consideration was being given to the role of private enterprise in television broadcasting.
You will accordingly be asked to make provision to enable the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to establish television stations in the Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver areas. My ministers have indicated to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that they are now prepared to consider applications for licenses of private television broadcasting stations which may be recommended by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-
Note that, if you please, Mr. Speaker, in the face of what the minister had to say this afternoon about the hands-off attitude followed by the government.
-to serve areas which could not be served at this time by public stations, with the objective of making television as widely available throughout


the country as may be feasible through appropriate co-operation between the corporation and private agencies.
I give that quotation from a lamentable passage in the speech from the throne.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the objective is to make television as widely available throughout the country as may be feasible, this policy enunciated in the terms of the paragraph I have just read is most certainly above all other policies calculated to defeat that objective. The policy of the government today, with the further outline given to the house by the minister on December 8, is just this: that the government will take unto the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation the choicest of all cities so far as revenues are concerned and size of population, and will then, in a grandiose gesture of generosity, permit private enterprise to operate in the smaller localities where there is the least chance of those communities being able to sustain the expense of television broadcasting. They follow that up, if you please, by saying that they will not allow two stations in any one place. That is a further development, Mr. Speaker, of the policy of the C.B.C. denying service to smaller communities.
Hear, hear.

There might be a great deal to be said, Mr. Speaker, for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation extending television service to areas where, if these absurd government controls were removed, service would still not be available. Does the government need to inaugurate costly service in communities where, if the government would remove the fetters it has imposed on private enterprise, there would be plenty of broadcasting available today? No, the government is not satisfied, and is so dominated by this monopolistic mania that has directed its policies from the beginning with regard to television, that it is going to use the money of the taxpayers of this country- be it a grant or be it a loan, for this purpose it is the money of the taxpayers of this country and they must pay it-to provide broadcasting under C.B.C. auspices in communities where, if the government would remove the fetters, there would be television service under private auspices and at private risk.
There is another aspect of this arrogant and obtuse policy, and it is this. Even in those areas into which the C.B.C. has entered, they will allow no other station. In Montreal and Toronto, the government says that these areas will be permitted only one television outlet. It is absurd, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the way television has developed in cities of the United States of comparable

size. But, sir, it suits the policy of this government that, because it has established one station in Montreal, it will allow nobody else to establish a station in Montreal; because it has established a C.B.C. station in Toronto, it will allow nobody else to establish a station in Toronto.
Well, here is the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie), who apparently is quite content to apply that policy of monopoly-
That is right.
-and I tell him that policy of monopoly is the policy that breeds regimentation, that breeds restriction in the exercise by our people of their rights as free men.
It breeds co-operation.

My hon. friend's idea may be to extend the size and power of government monopoly, but I can assure him that in that respect his ideas and mine are poles apart. I see no vindication of freedom in the assertion of government monopoly, and stupid government policy at that.
I have spoken of the way in which the government has thrown to private enterprise, in these smaller communities, a bone from which the C.B.C. has stripped all nourishment and meat. The people are going to be allowed to wait for television. What does it matter to this arrogant government if the people are made to wait for television service? A government that can say, "If we want to get away with it, who will stop us?" is obviously one that would say, "If we want to get away with sterilizing the development of television in this country, who will stop us?" It may be that we in the opposition are not numerically strong enough to stop them in this obtuse and wicked policy which they are following today. However, there is a day of reckoning ahead, and there is one sovereign force that can stop this government that thinks it can get away with anything it chooses. That sovereign force is the public at the ballot box. There is a day of reckoning ahead, Mr. Speaker.
I have one or two observations to make on two immediate aspects of this matter of television, Mr. Speaker. I did note that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in the tour he made of the west last September, was quick to speak of the way in which a new station was going to be set up in Vancouver. But it is worth recalling the following further report from Vancouver on September 3 as follows:
Mr. St. Laurent would not say how big a licence fee would be charged television set owners or
Committee on Broadcasting even, in fact, whether the operation will be financed on a licence fee basis. But he made it clear that nothing would be payable until after the end of the government's budget year on March 31.
"How the payment for these services should be made Is a question which is still under consideration", he said. "The government is, however, of the view that the remaining months of this fiscal year should be regarded as an experimental period in which experience will be gained in the handling of this new national service."
I do not profess to be a prophet, but I observe with some interest the date that the Prime Minister selected as the date before which there would be no licence fee imposed on television sets. I am just sufficiently familiar with the tactics of this government in previous years and in previous elections to be willing to hazard a guess that unless the government is driven by fear into postponing the election for a very long time-
Sit down.

-a licence fee for television receiving sets will not be established in the lifetime of the present parliament. It will be left until after the election, and it will be one of the many problems left on the doorstep of the incoming Progressive Conservative administration.
Oh, oh.

Let us look a little more closely into this subject, because the following day in Ottawa the chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was interrogated on this subject. Reference was made during the interrogation to the statement made by the Prime Minister in Vancouver the previous day, that parliament would be asked at the next session to authorize a loan to the C.B.C. for the construction of television stations on both coasts and the prairies. Let us bear this in mind when the government seeks to spur the appetites of those communities that do hope to receive television.
Today, A. D. Dunton, C.B.C. chairman, said it is difficult to forecast how long it will take to bring the stations into operation. It may be one year or two years from this fall.
When we hear the Minister of National Revenue today conjuring up hopes that the people of Vancouver are going to have television service before the end of 1953, and bearing in mind that in all likelihood we are going to have a general election in 1953, for my part I prefer to accept the informed prediction of the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as to when this service will be available in these communities, Vancouver, Halifax and Winnipeg. I note that he says it will be a year or two from the fall of 1952.
Then, sir, on this subject of development, I wish to mention what was said by the
1372	HOUSE OF
Committee on Broadcasting National Liberal Federation at its meeting three months ago. In a report by the Canadian Press from Ottawa on October 28, we read this:
On the heels erf its request yesterday for the abolition of radio licence fees, the 235-member council today asked for "the development of television in Canada by private enterprise along with the C.B.C."
The report also proceeds to say that "this resolution was adopted, according to delegates in the closed meeting, over the objections of revenue minister McCann". If the minister was not there in person, certainly his views were well understood. There you have a clear expression of opinion that is more closely related to the feelings of the people of this country than is the government today.
Now, sir, how good and how popular is the television service that the C.B.C. is providing in the two centres in which it is operating today at public expense? I have before me, sir, the reports of the Elliott-Haynes survey, a recognized survey which gives in parallel columns the degree of listener interest shown in the Toronto area by those listening to television programs over the C.B.C. as well as those over the private station which is available to Torontonians, WBEN-TV, from Buffalo. These are the results of listener interest according to this survey in September:

September 	
26-0	640October 	
22-2	77-8November 	
25-9	741December 	
22-9	771
You will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the people who have television receiving sets in the Toronto area prefer, in the proportion of seven to two, the programs they receive over the Buffalo stations to those available over the C.B.C. television station in Toronto. Will you also observe, Mr. Speaker, that the popularity of the C.B.C. station is not rising. It started out in September at 36 per cent; by December it had gone down to 22-9 per cent.
I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, and I want to be corrected if I am wrong. When discussing this new item of television, are you allowed to speak for an hour and twenty minutes?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) is not allowed to do so but the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) is.
I want a ruling, Mr. Speaker. Are you or are you not allowed to speak for an hour and twenty minutes?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member will find that, under standing order 37, the hon. member who has the floor is not limited to the usual forty minutes.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Fraser Valley is not enjoying what I have to say, I do not insist that he stay in the house. I will say this to him, however, since he is speaking about the length of speeches. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) confided in me this morning that he was going to speak about ten minutes; then he talked for about fifty-four minutes.
But he is a minister; the hon. member is not.
Oh, I see. Isn't that lovely? This totalitarian complex has affected even the hon. member for Fraser Valley.
I want an answer to my question.
However, I shall press on.
Why does the hon. member not be fair? I said that I would be ten minutes and I spoke for forty minutes.
Fifty-four by my count. I have another interesting report to which I wish to refer. It is the Gallup poll of public opinion.
Oh, oh.
I am not sorry to see that the hon. member for Fraser Valley has taken his stormy departure from the chamber.
If two more leave, we shall have to adjourn.

I wish to refer to this Gallup poll. I may say that I do not repose any unquestioning faith in Gallup polls; I do not say that they are infallible or that they are always right by any means, but I am interested in this particular one. It was issued on November 22, 1952, and it polls public opinion on this question:
As you probably know, at the present time, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (C.B.C.) has complete control of television programs and broadcasting in Canada. Do you think private stations should be allowed to broadcast television programs, or should it be left to the C.B.C.
Here is the vote:
Per cent
Private stations should	be allowed	 57
Should be left with C.B.C	 24
Qualified opinion	 3
No opinion	 16
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, you clearly see that on the part of those who were prepared to

express a clear-cut opinion on this subject, 57 out of every 81 said they wanted private development of television.
Is that in Ontario?

No, that is a national poll.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make reference to a point which has been made by the minister about what has been done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the development of Canadian talent; and so far as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are developing Canadian talent they will certainly have my support in so doing. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is not encouraging the development of Canadian talent when it stifles the development of television in the way it has been doing. Lest anyone should think that the minister could by any chance be right in pretending that radio artists support this exclusive and monopolistic policy of the C.B.C. and the government, I read this press release of a statement issued by the agent of the American federation of radio artists, A.F.L., at Windsor on July 6. It states:
Canadian radio artists cannot tail to be concerned by the statement attributed to revenue minister McCann on Friday, in which he was reported to have told the House of Commons that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will not license privately-owned television stations until it has stations of its own operating in every province of Canada.
This will have the effect of depriving Canadian talent in most regions of all opportunities of gaining experience and a livelihood in this new medium.
It means, furthermore, that for years to come, any Canadian performer will be entirely at the mercy of the C.B.C. as to whether he appears in television at all, for if the C.B.C. is unable to employ him, or worse still, if he incurs its disapprobation, he will be deprived of any other outlet for his talents. Should this view appear too pessimistic, it must be regarded in the light of experience with Canadian radio and the C.B.C.
Since the establishment of publicly-owned radio in Canada in 1932 under the C.B.C.'s predecessor, the Canadian Radio Commission, it has taken twenty years for the system to achieve relatively complete coverage of the country as a whole, with the means at its disposal.
If the extension of television service is to be similarly delayed, and private stations afforded no opportunity of entering the field, it may be assumed that many of today's radio performers will be lucky if their grandchildren see them on television.
Since it has been indicated that the C.B.C. will afford the advertising agencies less latitude than exists in radio in producing and presumably in casting their sponsors' programs, the preservation of a monopoly in the hands of one body for perhaps twenty years will further deprive the art of the benefits of healthy competition.
When we are forced to rely on distilleries for the encouragement of Canadian theatre, it appears strange that the enormously greater costs of television are expected to be met from the public
Fair Employment Practices purse when there are others willing and ready to assume the burden. We are already six years behind on this continent, and twelve years behind Great Britain where, it is interesting to note, parliament has approved the eventual entry into television of private enterprise, after thirty years of state monopoly in sound and television broadcasting.
This is my final observation, Mr. Speaker.

The Massey royal commission recommended that we have our own development of Canadian talent on Canadian programs. What has become of the Massey report now?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 2, to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the consideration of this bill was last before the house I had begun a few remarks in relation to it. When the debate adjourned I had been referring to this legislation and to the history of the consideration of similar bills in this house. I had pointed out that it was my view, and a view shared by many hon. members, that a subject matter of this kind was something that should be left to the process of collective bargaining. I had pointed out that my main concern with regard to this matter was as it affected the employees of our two great national railway systems, and the steps I had taken in an attempt to do what I could to see that both parties concerned, management and labour in this particular industry, considered their positions with respect to the check-off from that point of view rather than to await or expect any legislative action on the part of this parliament to deal with it.
In his very complete and excellent speech on this matter the last day the house considered it, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cote) referred to the recent settlement of differences between the railway management and the non-operating employees, and the new contract which had been entered into between the railways and the unions representing those classifications of their employees; and he pointed out that as one of the terms of this recent agreement the employees had been granted a form of union security, the check-off, on what I believe to be a very much more favourable and more satisfactory basis than would be provided under the provisions of the enactment which

is before the house this afternoon and which in virtually identical form has been before this house in previous sessions.
I believe that the conclusion of this agreement between the railways and the unions representing their non-operating employees is a vindication of the position that has been taken in this matter by the Minister of Labour and by hon. members who have indicated views similar to those expressed by him and by the parliamentary assistant. It is certainly a vindication of the position of a former minister of labour, the late Humphrey Mitchell. I remember very well the excellent way in which the late Mr. Mitchell, when he was responsible for the Department of Labour, dealt with matters of this kind, not only in this house but in the committee which during 1947 and 1948 considered with such care the provisions of the national labour code which was enacted into law by this house in 1948. I know we all enjoyed the rather rare but always interesting contributions that Humphrey Mitchell used to make to the debates in this house. He spoke very forcefully indeed on a measure similar to this one on several occasions during my time here in parliament.
It must be obvious to all who are interested in and understand the labour movement that the position he took in those days has certainly been vindicated by the events of this year which were referred to in his speech the other evening by the parliamentary assistant. It is a vindication also, I believe, of the attitude that has been taken in this house and expressed on a number of occasions by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald), who I think has as much personal experience in labour matters as any hon. member.
The hon. member for Edmonton East has expressed his views on this particular proposal on several occasions. I was delighted to know that when speaking earlier in this debate he was able to point out how satisfied he was with the kind of union security which he had hoped for, and for which he had worked, and which he urged had been brought about by the process of collective bargaining. He expressed his satisfaction that this house had never fallen into what he considered would have been the error and which I consider would be the error of legislating into effect a form of union check-off which would not give the kind of security desired by him, by other hon. members and by other people who believe in the value and the strength and the service of labour unions, the kind of union security to which they are entitled and for which they should work.

I think that position, the position of the hon. member for Edmonton East, the position of the late Humphrey Mitchell, the position of the present Minister of Labour, the position of the parliamentary assistant and others, which has been so clearly stated in the house, is the correct one, and it is the position which I believe receives the support of a very large majority of the members of unions who will be affected by legislation of this kind.
The late Humphrey Mitchell always used to say that what governments can give governments can take away, and he did not want to see essential elements of working conditions, conditions of labour and all that sort of thing, which he regarded as matters for collective bargaining, brought into the realm of the kind of thing about which we legislate in parliament.
I support that view. That is the reason for the stand I have expressed on many occasions in the house, and which I repeat today. I think the probabilities are-and I would hope this would occur-that the step taken to establish the Rand formula check-off for the non-operating unions of the railways will gradually be extended and adopted in respect of other employees who would be affected by this legislation. I should think that, in that event, the end result would be much more favourable, both from the point of view of labour and of management, in all the industries which come under the provisions of our national labour code.
In referring to the national labour code I think I should draw attention to the interesting and, I think, valuable suggestion made by the parliamentary assistant in his speech on this bill, to which I have already referred. He suggested that as the labour code was enacted into law by parliament in 1948, and a period of five years from that time will have elapsed shortly, consideration should be given to having the legislation referred to the committee on industrial relations at some early date so the committee could study the legislation in the light of the five years of experience we have had and management and labour have had in the working of that labour code.

Perhaps the hon. member has more information than I have about future events of that kind. However, I do not think our views on whether or not this is a valuable suggestion would depend upon the intervention of an election. I should think most members would be prepared to consider that proposal as one which could be brought into effect at an appropriate time, whether or not there should be an election in the meantime.
Industrial Relations
My only purpose in calling it to the attention of the house is to record my support of that suggestion, and I would hope that other hon. members who may take part in the debate would indicate whether they think this suggestion merits consideration or otherwise. It appears to me that the committee on industrial relations is the proper one to deal with matters of this kind; and a reference of the labour code to the committee, with proper publicity and some warning, would give all interested parties an opportunity to prepare submissions which could be placed before the committee. In this way a thorough and complete study could be made of the legislation as it stands on the statute books, and an investigation could be made as to the way in which it has operated. I am sure we would receive very valuable suggestions which we could use as an indication of amendments which might be made to improve or to expand the present provisions.
The proposal of the hon. member who sponsors the bill is, as has been pointed out, one which amounts to an ad hoc amendment of the labour code, in a way which obviously would not be in accord with the general scheme and principle of the legislation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), who immediately preceded me in the debate, as I understood him attempted to make the point that the opening sections of the labour code do, in fact, dictate to both management and labour what must be done and that, in effect, these sections are achieving the same kind of imposition of procedures on both management and labour as would flow from our putting into legislative form a proposal for the check-off, or some other form of union security.
I would point out to the hon. member that in my view there is a very wide difference between the provisions of legislation which creates the necessary machinery for two parties to come together to bargain on matters of common interest, and any attempt by a legislature or any other authority to dictate the terms of an agreement which would be entered into between those parties, using that particular mechanism. It is just as if our general law, which provides for the enforceability of contracts, were to be amended to require that a certain provision be a part of every contract in order that it might be enforceable.
There is a great difference between the setting up of machinery by the appropriate government authority to do certain things, and the imposition by a government authority of certain things that must be done through that machinery. It is for that reason that I think this proposal is contrary to the underlying principle of our labour code, and that we

Industrial Relations
should not amend the labour code in this regard without considering the whole basis of our legislation and, if necessary, making appropriate changes in its principle to permit us properly to adopt suggestions of this kind.
That is the sort of study that I think the committee could give to this legislation. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will be a member of that committee, and that his advice and arguments will be of great assistance to the committee in coming to a conclusion. I see that the hon. member wishes to ask a question.
