subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to prolong the debate on this matter because I have spoken on this question several times. This is not the first time this bill has come before the house. I should say that on each occasion it has come before us we have supported it for a number of obvious reasons which I shall give in a few minutes.

It has been said by speakers on the government side of the house that the proper way to deal with a bill of this kind is to refer it to the industrial relations committee. I recall back in 1948 that this very question came up before the committee. Of course I realize that the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) was not minister at that time, the minister then being the late Hon. Humphrey Mitchell.
This question has been given lengthy consideration in the committee on a number of occasions. I remember it was given a thorough going over in the industrial relations committee in 1948, and the committee voted in favour of having a voluntary revocable checkoff provision included in the legislation. When the bill was reported back to the house it was the then minister of labour who caused that provision to be rescinded. If the same attitude is to be taken when the committee is next set up as was taken at that time, no good purpose can be served in even having it referred to the committee. The attitude of the government, as it has been presented to us during this debate, does not seem to have changed from what it was at that time.
I cannot understand why there should be so much government objection to having a voluntary revocable check-off provision in our labour code. The compulsory check-off is included in the legislation in Alberta having to do with our teachers. To my knowledge there has never been any objection either from teachers' organizations, from school boards or from anyone else about that legislation. I understand that similar legislation has worked quite satisfactorily in Saskatchewan.
I think I am safe in saying that all of the mining contracts in Alberta contain a voluntary revocable check-off provision. It is true that that is not by legislation but by negotiation, but the provision is there just the same and there has been no complaint in that regard. I feel quite sure there would be no complaint in connection with the mining contracts if that provision were in the legislation. Both types, the compulsory check-off and the voluntary check-off, are working there, and certainly no objection has ever been raised.
It is all very well to say that this should be done by negotiation. The government has pointed to the new contract which was entered into on December 19 between the nonoperating employees and the railroads as indicating the method that should be followed. Mr. Speaker, as I well remember when I was teaching in the province of Alberta, there were a very small number of us who continued to pay our fees to the Alberta teachers'
Industrial Relations
organization. A great many of those people who were teaching-and this applies to all types of labour-would only pay their dues when they found themselves in need of assistance from the association. That point should be remembered.
Anyone who has had anything to do with labour organizations, be they teachers or miners, knows that you just cannot carry on an organization without proper financial assistance. The railways say: Well, it should be a matter of negotiation and the unions should collect their own fees; but, mind you, the railways themselves are in a very preferred position when it comes to getting their financial revenue. They even have the interest on their investment guaranteed by legislation. They should be the last people in the world to object to the voluntary revocable check-off. Their profits are guaranteed by legislation. Every time there comes a raise in pay they just come back to the government and say, "Well, this is it. You will have to give us higher freight rates in order to meet these obligations."
It is most difficult indeed for any workers' organizations to carry on unless they have a very definite means of getting financial assistance. There is no doubt in anyone's mind that the labour organizations have given in the past and are now giving a service to their members which has resulted in raising their standard of living very materially. It is they who have improved the working conditions of working people in this country more than any other type of organization. Everyone acknowledges that, and these unions can only function if they have some means of raising the necessary funds to carry on, They have found by experience that it is most difficult to carry on in the manner in which the government would have them carry on.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to talk this thing out. I have no objection whatever to its being referred to a committee, though I am a little bit dubious about what action will be taken on it there, when I well know that a majority of members on the committee will be Liberal members who favour the government's stand on this question. However, I suppose it is the proper place for it to be referred; therefore I am not taking any more time except to say that I am in favour of it, and if it should come to a vote, I shall vote in favour of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I had no intention of making my maiden speech tonight, and I hope that you will not consider the few opinions I am

Industrial Relations
about to express as being my maiden speech in this house.
(Text):
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that I hope no one will take these few remarks as being my maiden speech. However, industrial relations is a question that does interest me particularly. I think it is a rather important subject, and I would like to voice a few of my opinions.
I do not believe that anyone has really been opposed to the voluntary revocable check-off proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). There is nothing radically wrong with the principle, and no one on this side of the house objects to it. However, there can be some question about its efficiency. As the hon. member himself has stated, this particular principle of the voluntary revocable check-off does exist in most of the provinces. As it is applied in practically all industries where unions are authorized by their respective labour commissioners, I do not believe that anything would be added by having federal legislation on the subject. As the hon. member says, the motion can do no more than give a minimum amount of union security, so the purpose of the motion itself would not avail a great deal for union security of which everyone is in favour. The particular principle already exists in the different provinces and is applied in practically all the large industries of the provinces.
There is one other question which to my mind is rather important, and it is a question of policy. I have not been here sufficiently long to know what the exact policy of the government is on this subject but I personally feel that the federal legislature, as a matter of principle, should keep out of business and industry as much as it possibly can. I am not alone in saying this. If you will permit me, I would like to read some pertinent remarks that I have taken from the Montreal Gazette of January 21, 1953, entitled "Hands off Industry-Chamber".
Canada's businessmen today asked the federal government to keep its fingers out of industry as much as possible.
Further down it says that:
-in Canada the relationship between business and government is something unique in the world, valuable and worth keeping.
To maintain this relationship business should refrain from looking to the government for solution of its problems and difficulties-
I believe there is much in that statement. I believe it is a fundamental principle, and that we could condense it by saying that when trouble arises between unions and employers it should be settled between themselves if at all possible. Afterward, if the parties cannot
JMr. Cardin.]
come to any agreement, the most natural person or organization that should be consulted or that should intervene is the provincial government. That has been done. In most labour codes they have the subject matter of today's discussion, a section regarding the voluntary revocable check-off. It is the parties I have mentioned, to my mind, whose duty it should be to solve the problems of industry in the different provinces. There they know more of the problems of the particular industry than the federal government knows.
That is what I have to offer by way of comment on this motion. I believe that, as a matter of policy, the federal government should only in case of absolute necessity, but not as a general practice or policy, invade the field of industry, which to my mind should be left under the control of the provincial governments. May I say that since the voluntary revocable check-off exists in the provinces; since it applies to most industries throughout Canada; since it can give only a minimum amount of union security, then I do not see any point in passing this bill. I feel that I should vote against such a measure.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), who has just taken his seat, put his finger on the crux of this situation. He has pointed out that many of the provinces have provided for the voluntary revocable check-off in industries over which the provinces have jurisdiction. The federal labour code applies to those industries which are interprovincial in character, and therefore do not come within the legislative competence of the provincial governments. The people who are employed in those industries, such as communications and so forth, are therefore a group of people who might be termed second-class citizens, because of the fact that they do not come under provincial jurisdiction, and because of the fact that their unions have to deal on a national basis for many of their benefits.
Now, I believe the most important reason for the voluntary revocable check-off is that it does bring the employer and employee together on a basis of recognition. While forcing the employer to give recognition to the union, after a time it removes the feeling of animosity that existed before this measure of security was obtained. When an employee makes an assignment of his wages for any other purpose, it has been honoured by the employer. In the case of income tax collections for the federal government it is not even necessary to make a written assignment of your wages. The assignment of a portion

of an employee's wages each month for the payment of bonds has been accepted as a good policy. Deductions are made for other purposes, such as housing loans and welfare societies; and in cases where employees band together for the purpose of insuring their health, they may have the premiums deducted from their wages. When an employer refuses to honour a written assignment for another body, an organization just as important as the employer organization, then it necessarily causes a feeling of resentment and does not act in the best interests of labour relations. Some employers refuse to accept this principle, yet in the provinces where the principle has been accepted we find the very best of labour relations and the unions enjoy some measure of security.
I would say to the house that there is a very limited amount of compulsion in the voluntary revocable check-off. I should like to read into the record a section of an agreement which is in force between the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company and local 651 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers. I should like to quote section B of article 21, but before doing so perhaps I should quote section A:
The company shall honour a written assignment of wages to the union.
As I pointed out before, that gives a measure of recognition and leads to harmony between the company and the employees. The company honours other assignments, so it agrees to honour an assignment of wages for union purposes.
Section B reads as follows:
An assignment pursuant to section A shall be substantially in the following form:
To The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada Limited.
Until this authority is revoked by me in writing, I hereby authorize you to deduct from my wages and pay to local 651 of the international union of mine, mill and smelter workers fees in the amounts following.
That is the assignment which, under this legislation, would require an employer to deduct union dues. For those who maintain that there would be less compulsion if this matter were left entirely to negotiation between the company and the employees, I should like to read a quotation concerning union security by Chief Justice Sloan. I understand that the union had asked for a union shop, and the matter was referred to a mediation committee headed by Gordon Sloan, Chief Justice of British Columbia. As a consequence of the decision of that committee, the following article now appears in this agreement from which I have quoted:
The company shall during the life of this agreement deduct, as a condition of each employee's
Committee on Broadcasting continued employment, the sum of $2 from the first pay cheque due in each calendar month to each such employee and remit the same prior to the tenth day of the month following the month in which such deduction is made, to the financial secretary of the union. The company will, at the time of making each such payment to the financial secretary of the union, name the employees from whose pay such payment has been deducted.
This has become known as the Sloan formula, and is very similar to the Rand formula which has been adopted in some industries in Ontario. I simply wanted to point out the difference between this voluntary revocable check-off and other forms of union security. In common with many other Liberal members, perhaps all the Liberal members from British Columbia, I believe that this legislation will be a benefit to those in industries affected by it, and that it should pass at this time.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. McCann that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That a select committee be appointed on broadcasting to consider the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and to review the policies and aims of the corporation and its regulations, revenues, expenditures and development with power to examine and inquire into the matters and things herein referred to and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, and to send for persons, papers and records; that the committee have power to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable or necessary; that the committee have power to meet while the house is sitting; that the committee shall consist of the following members:	Messrs. Beaudry, Boisvert,
Breton, Carter, Courtemanche, Decore, Diefen-baker, Dinsdale, Fleming, Fulton, Gauthier (Port-neuf), Gauthier (Sudbury), Hansell, Henry, Jones,

Committee on Broadcasting Kirk (Digby-Yarmouth), Knight, MacLean (Queens), McCann, Murray (Cariboo), Mutch, Richard (Ottawa East), Riley, Robinson, Smith (Moose Mountain), and Whitman. That standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.

Mr. Speaker, may I have your indulgence for a moment. Matters have arisen during the dinner recess which make it desirable that those of my colleagues and I who can be out of the house, without interfering with the business here, do give those matters consideration. I apologize to our colleagues in the house for our absenting ourselves, but I am sure there will be a full quorum.
We will take care of it.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) had been deploring the monopolistic position of the C.B.C. vis-a-vis the private radio stations in Canada. We of course cannot agree with the hon. member for Eglinton in that regard. As to the report of the royal commission, we find ourselves in agreement with it rather than opposed to it.
In the matter of the private stations I think our view would be expressed by that report at page 283, where it says:
The principal grievance of the private broadcasters is based, it seems to us, on a false assumption that broadcasting in Canada is an industry. Broadcasting in Canada, in our view, is a public service directed and controlled in the public interest by a body responsible to parliament.
I would suggest, sir, that the C.B.C. is not a competitor, in the ordinary sense in which that word is used, of the private radio stations. It is not just one rival amidst a group of rivals. At page 284 the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences has this to say, which expresses our view:
The statement that the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is at once their judge and their business rival implies a view of the national system which has no foundation in law, and which has never been accepted by parliamentary committees or by the general public.
The broadcasting set-up that we have in Canada was established, as hon. members know, by the government of the late Ft. B. Bennett in the following terms as reported at page 2826 of Hansard of 1932:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide for the constitution of a commission to be known as the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission, for the purpose of acquiring, operating, regulating and controlling radio broadcasting in Canada.
Then there is the idea of an independent regulating authority to which the private stations would appeal if they found it necessary, presumably against decisions taken in


regard to them by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself. I am afraid we cannot even go as far as that, because that again would do the very thing which it has been suggested in the quotations I have read should not be done, namely bring the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation down to the level of those private stations. By that action you would destroy the possibility of public radio doing a good job for the people of Canada. You would bring down to the level where it would be merely the commercial rival of the private stations, a corporation which, according to the purpose of the act passed and the resolution which I have read, was to have as one of its functions the actual control of radio broadcasting in Canada. You will notice that I did not use the term "public ownership". I said "public control" because as I see it the private stations have a very distinct and useful function in radio broadcasting in Canada, but that I shall develop in a minute or two.
The result of the setting up of such a regulatory body would change the whole function of the C.B.C. You would then have the picture of the C.B.C., which functions as a regulatory body according to the act, being in the position where it would have to compete for business with the private stations, and by so doing and by that concession to commercialism, as I see it, there would be a consequent and growing inferiority in the matter of programs.
We welcome the setting up of such a committee as is envisaged in the present resolution, in which we may review the work and activities of the C.B.C. We think it is a democratic process to have a corporation of this kind whose actions can be scrutinized year by year by the elected representatives of the people.
In the name of my party I would reiterate our position in the matter of public control of that body. As they were meant to do, and in conformity with their proper function, private stations have given good service in various places across Canada. I think there is a place for them, particularly in a country as widespread and as far-flung as Canada. But we must not forget that the privileges private stations have enjoyed have not been given to them as of right but, as it were, as an act of grace; and they must not presume upon that fact. They are not rights at all, in terms of the broadcasting set-up, but rather strength which they have accumulated by that act of grace on the part of the Canadian people.

Our friends in the private radio stations talk a good deal about freedom of speech.
I would imagine that all hon. members would favour that. But in commercial broadcasting, by the very nature of things work is done for private profit. Most of the time allotted by these stations has to do with the making of money, and that is perfectly all right for a private station. The general result, however, is-and I believe I am correct when I say "is" -certainly the general result would be, under the set-up as they see it, too great an allotment of commercial time, with a resulting disadvantage along other lines.
Surely there must be some equitable division of time allotted for political broadcasts. That is to say, there should be an allotment of time which would not be dependent upon the possession of money, or the lack of it, as might well be the case in respect of some political parties. Under a system of public control surely we would expect a situation wherein all public opinion would be represented; and we would see to it-as indeed we are seeing to it-that in broadcasts there would be represented all shades of opinion, and that these opinions might be aired with justice and equity. Both sides of any question would be heard.
I suggest that if there is a purely commercial set-up it is only natural and human that those who have the most money to buy radio time would have the greater use of radio. On the other hand those who had not the money would not be able to avail themselves of radio time. That would be the ultimate conclusion under a broadcasting system controlled completely and totally by private hands rather than in the public interest or, as we have it today, under mixed public and private control.
In the middle west programs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation are very popular indeed. I can speak, of course, more particularly of that part of the west from which I come. Programs such as "Farm Forum", the Wednesday night program, and others are received with great favour. We know there is some criticism of the C.B.C. I have never known anything worth while against which there was not a good deal of criticism. This would apply not only to an organization but also to a man in public life.
I realize there is some criticism of the C.B.C. as an agency under public control. We suggest, however, that much of that criticism is the result of propaganda-very efficient propaganda-carried on by those who would profit by a lessening of that control.
I am glad the C.B.C. gives opportunity for the development of local talent in the arts of music and literature. I believe I would be
Committee on Broadcasting expected to say that in my part of Canada there is a gap in the C.B.C. service, and I refer to the area in the heart of Saskatchewan. I welcome the setting up of the committee because it provides an opportunity to question officials of the C.B.C. as to when they are going to bring to the prairies the production studio we have been promised. We have been told by those who plan such things for the C.B.C. that this matter has first priority. I shall carry my representations a little further and say that my own city of Saskatoon would be the ideal location for such a production unit. I shall not develop this point at greater length, because it was not my purpose in rising this evening to do so. Let me point out briefly, however, that geographically Saskatoon is in the centre of the province, it is the centre of culture in the province and is the seat of the provincial university.
But enough about local matters. Let us pass on for a moment to television. When compared with radio, television has even greater powers for good or evil, if I may so describe those powers. Because the television channels are much less numerous I should think that public control would be even more essential.
As one who has interested himself in educational matters, and particularly the guidance of young people, I have been interested in statistics from the United States which show the number of hours that children in that country, either with or without their parents' consent, spend watching television. Let me say at once that if our television programs are not a good deal better than some I have seen in the United States, or coming from that country, so far as the youth of our country are concerned we would be better without it.
This does not mean that we are not able to build good programs. On the contrary it seems to me that it is simply a matter of taste, and of control by people in charge who will give us the kind of programs we want. I suggest that no group of people are better qualified to give that control than are the people's representatives in the House of Commons.
Let me compare programs from the United States with those I have seen in Great Britain. Let me admit at once that I did not see many over there, but I did see some. Mr. Speaker, we in this corner of the house are happy to support the motion for the setting up this year of a radio committee. In fact in previous times we have advocated that this should be a standing committee.
I should like to say a few words in reply to the minister who spoke this afternoon. For the most part we agree with many of the observations which the minister made. In this connection may I say that we are not opponents of the C.B.C. in the sense of opposing the corporation. We like to be fair in all things. I am not going to stand here this evening and rip the C.B.C. to pieces, and I certainly am not desirous of bringing this matter into the general political arena.
We believe that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has a very important place in radio in Caiufia. We do not oppose the C.B.C., but we do oppose certain radio policies which have been written into the laws- of


this country. We maintain that it is the law of the country affecting radio policies that needs to be changed. We believe that the C.B.C., being in a competitive radio field, should not have powers of regulation and control.
This afternoon the minister stated that many people and many powerful organizations in Canada had sent in resolutions of commendation of the present radio policy and the work of the C.B.C. As far as commendation of the corporation is concerned, perhaps that is all to the good. The minister told us also that there was some criticism, and that too is to the good. I do not think even the C.B.C. would say that criticism was not sometimes good. However, there is a difference between criticism of radio policy that might be levelled at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and what might be levelled at independent sponsors of radio.
Criticism levelled at an independent sponsor indicates to that sponsor that he must be ready to adjust his program, or else. That is not necessarily so when criticism is levelled at the government-owned and subsidized corporation. It does not necessarily have to pay a great deal of attention to such criticism because after all the life of the corporation is dependent to a large extent upon the public treasury. That difference in respect to criticism I think should be noted.
There is another thing I should like to say in respect to the minister's observations this afternoon. He had a good deal to say about the virtues of broadcasting, but I would remind him that much of what he said, which I suppose he intended to apply to the corporation, could be said about broadcasting in the independent field of radio. Those virtues can be applied to all radio; they are not confined to the publicly-owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I do wish to say a word about what I consider to be the proposed tightening up of regulations affecting independent stations in respect to religious broadcasting and about any proposed changes that may be under consideration for tightening the regulations in respect to political broadcasts. There is one responsibility that the publicly-owned broadcasting company has, and it is a responsibility that we must not forget. It is a responsibility toward the homes and the family life of our Canadian citizens. Let us remember that every radio program or television program goes into the homes of our citizens, and that is a very, very important thing. Let us not forget that as it is such a powerful medium for shaping public thought and public morals, radio should be guarded with the greatest of jealousy to see that the programs which go into our homes will tend to elevate and bring our Canadian nation to a place of respectability.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I suppose we should get through with this foolishness. However, it is not all foolishness. Some of the things I have been talking about are in reality pretty serious, and that is freedom of expression, freedom on behalf of the public to support that which they choose to support with their pocketbooks. Under the present system they are forced to support with their pocketbooks perhaps something they do not like, because we tax the people not only in


radio licences but every time we have to subsidize the C.B.C., whether the people like it or not. The one thing that we can keep free is the people's freedom to support financially the things they want to support.
I say these things are serious to me. I think they are serious to the Canadian people. They are serious if they will think them through. May I say to the minister that we shall support his resolution setting up the committee. I can also say to him that he will find us co-operative in attempting to make suggestions and bring out the truth in order to give the Canadian people the best type of broadcasting and television that is possible in Canada.

Since I will be a member of the committee that is to be set up soon, and since I have been a member of radio committees since 1945, I think I may be permitted to say a few words on this matter. In the past we have had pretty interesting sessions of radio committees, during which I have sometimes criticized the C.B.C. In that criticism I have tried to be as constructive as possible and as pleasant as possible, but at the same time I have tried to speak my mind frankly, and I have tried to help not only the C.B.C. but [DOT] the people of Canada at large.
I believe that with the good co-operation of the House of Commons and of the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation-I did not mention the co-operation of the minister because we have had that for a long time-we can arrive at such an achievement as will give the people of Canada almost complete satisfaction in the operation of this publicly-owned service.
This afternoon we heard some criticism of a couple of scripts put on by the C.B.C., especially in the west. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) referred to a dialogue between a Mr. McGatt and an Eskimo. He concluded that this dialogue showed that the person who was carrying on the dialogue with the Eskimo was giving the impression that he was criticizing Christianity. I think the hon. member for Eglinton was a little lacking in a sense of humour. He did not quite catch the humour in the dialogue between the Eskimo and the other person.
He also criticized a script read by somebody who was talking about the present situation in Asia. The hon. member criticized that script because he said the speaker was putting the blame on the back and shoulders of the United States, saying that the United States was responsible for the present situation in Asia. May I tell my hon. friend that I recently read a book on the matter written

by a good Englishman from England. The whole book consisted of a series of statements having to do with the responsibility of Britain, the United States, France, and the Netherlands for the present situation in Asia. Because the writer said that, I do not believe we should be surprised if Russia takes advantage of the present situation, or think he was being vehemently critical especially of the United States. I believe the speaker on the radio was just stating facts, and that he was saying to his listeners that naturally the U.S.S.R., which is so close to that part of Asia, has been taking advantage of the present situation and of the mistakes made in the past by the powers that are foreign to Asia.
I want it perfectly understood that if I am supporting the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the setting up of this committee and most of the policies of the C.B.C., I am not opposing altogether at the same time all the requests and the points of view of the privately-owned stations. No, I think they have their own interests to take care of, their own interests to defend. I think their criticism is welcome provided that it is constructive, and is offered in a pleasant way. I do not oppose them altogether. I say that at the present time Canada needs this organization, the C.B.C., functioning as it does presently under the direction and administration of the board of directors.
Of course sometimes regulations have to be passed which do not please everyone. Scripts have been put on the air of which, at times, I have not approved. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) will remember my criticism of the scripts dealing with Bertrand Russell and Anna Freud. I believe that took place either last year or the year before. I strongly opposed the presentation of the views held by those people. I would still oppose any such presentation; and every time a script of that kind is brought to my attention I shall oppose it. My criticism was that those scripts should not have been presented on the air, especially over the C.B.C. stations.
But if there have been mistakes made by the C.B.C., I am sure that mistakes have been made, too, by the privately-owned stations. We must not heap all the sins of the world on the shoulders of the directors of the publicly-owned organization. We must establish a dividing line of responsibility between the privately-owned and publicly-owned systems.

I think my hon. friend would agree, though, that when an objectionable script is used, it is much more serious when
Committee on Broadcasting it is put over the national network of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation than if put out only over some private stations.

That would
depend on certain things, of course. It would be most important that scripts of that kind should not be put on the air from a powerful privately-owned station serving, we will say, a million or half a million people. I would understand, of course, that if these objectionable lectures are put on the air over the national network they would reach more people than they would if put out over a privately-owned station, even though a big one.
I must repeat, however, that mistakes have not been made only on one side; the sins have not been committed only by the C.B.C. Sins and mistakes have been committed by the privately-owned stations, too; and my hon. friend knows that.
Although in the past I have criticized what has been done by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, I still maintain that we need it. It is important that the operations of the corporation shall continue. It is important that this publicly-owned system shall continue to give the good service it has given the people of Canada in the past. There can be no question about that.
Upon reading the Massey report I found three good reasons for supporting broadcasting by the C.B.C. One of these reasons is that Canada has a small and scattered population in a vast area. Second, this population is clustered along the rim of another country many times more populous and of far greater economic strength. The third reason is that the majority of Canadians share their mother tongue with that neighbour, and this leads to a peculiarly close and intimate relationship. We are close to the United States.
Let us suppose that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did not exist. My view is that if it were not in existence at this time it would have to be created at once, due to the vast financial strength of our neighbour to the south. If we did not have good programs put out by the C.B.C., neighbouring stations in the United States would draw Canadian listeners.
The C.B.C. is managed by human beings, and it cannot be perfect. At the same time, the privately-owned stations are in the same position; they are bound to make mistakes, too. But anyone who has a reasonable knowledge of radio broadcasting throughout the world will admit that the organization of the C.B.C., not only in Montreal but in the whole of Canada, is second to none in

Committee on Broadcasting the world. My hon. friends have seen that organization in Montreal, and they know that what I say it true.
We are a small population in a vast area. For example, one station in the city of New York can reach a population equal to that of Canada. Large amounts of money can flow into the purse of a privately-owned station in that city, because it will have great numbers of listeners, and the commercial material in the broadcasts can be made more interesting. Those who advertise over such a station realize that the more people who listen, the greater will be the results from advertising.
In Great Britain the British Broadcasting Corporation reaches a population of 50 million through the use of 975 miles of landline. In Canada we require 15,000 miles of telegraph and telephone lines to provide a national broadcasting service to our 14 million people. One can easily understand the difficulties which confronted the C.B.C. when it was created in 1936. Imagine the courage and far-sightedness that must have been exercised by the organizers of this publicly-owned organization. At first sight they had to realize that we must have some organization capable of covering large and far-removed areas. The privately-owned stations would not be interested because, from such areas, they could not derive enough income to cover their operational expenses.
I believe we can imagine what would have happened by taking the railways as an example. Perhaps the cheapest way of communication by rail between Montreal and Winnipeg could have been by way of Chicago. Not only would it have been cheaper; it would have been easier, and perhaps shorter. But it would not have been an all-Canadian railway system. To have that all-Canadian route we had to have help from public funds, as well as some kind of arrangement with the privately-owned system.
In radio the condition has been the same. We had to have the co-operation and help of both the publicly-owned and privately-owned systems in order to provide more facilities for those who wanted to go into this business. They needed sufficient facilities in order to start a very profitable business. That is what happened. No one can say that the C.B.C. has put privately-owned stations out of business since its inception. The number of privately-owned stations in Canada at the present time is proof that after all the regulations of the C.B.C. are not as stringent as some say they are and will continue to say they are.
There is another angle from which this problem of radio broadcasting can be approached, the angle concerning education,

culture and even national unity. Because of our nearness to the United States we are exposed to and endangered by its powerful financial organization. We must realize that we have something to preserve in our culture which is superior because of its duality. We must not allow United States culture to get the best of our listeners in Canada. Our listeners should not be subjected to the expansion of United States culture and at the same time forget our Canadian culture which has been achieved through Providence and because of the courage and broad-mindedness of the two principal races who have lived in Canada since the opening up of this country. The Massey report has this to say at page 276:
On the other hand, radio, as one of the most powerful means of education, may be regarded as a social influence too potent and too perilous to be ignored by the state which, in modern times, increasingly has assumed responsibility for the welfare of its citizens.
Those who invest money in broadcasting do not want to lose what they have invested. It is normal that they should want it to be a paying proposition, and there should be no quarrel about that. In order to make the greater profit they want to serve as many people as possible so that what they advertise will be most interesting. That is natural and normal. But who is to cover the vast areas with small populations if the C.B.C. is done away with? No one will cover those areas because it will not be a paying proposition to broadcast there. The C.B.C. has entered that field. I am sure that all rightthinking Canadians, those who do not want to offer futile criticism, will agree with me when I say that if the C.B.C. had not been created it would have to be created now because we need it in the worst way.
I admit that the publicly-owned system is supported by the taxpayers' money, and that that money should be spent according to their best wishes. The C.B.C. has made mistakes, and in the past I have offered criticism of its operations. I may have criticism to offer in the future. But I believe that in the long run the C.B.C. has a most commendable record as far as its work and achievements are concerned. I am sure the people of Canada at large support the work done by the C.B.C. for the Canadian people.
I am sure that I will not scandalize anyone when I say that I shall support the motion. I am not a socialist, nor do I believe that the more we have in the way of publicly-owned enterprise, the better it will be. I am in favour of private enterprise. But in certain fields, in this instance the broadcasting field,

I believe that a government-owned system is best. In that way the people are given the best programs possible.
The other day I read an article criticizing the new regulations about the use of Canadian talent. Canada is an ant-hill of talent and I think the more of this talent that is used, the better it will be for Canada and the more we will be doing to preserve our duality of culture.
I repeat that I will support the setting up of a committee. As far as my conscience allows me to do so, I will support the C.B.C. in the future. But I shall hold myself free, as we do in the Liberal party, to criticize when I think criticism should be made.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Oh, oh.
My hon. friend says, "oh, oh." I understand that "oh, oh", because it comes from the whip of the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house has listened with interest and in large measure with approval to the most thoughtful speech just delivered by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). One may disagree with some of his ideas, but at the same time I think we must admire an attitude which is so fair and reasonable in the discussion of this problem, as the hon. member has exhibited on other occasions in the past.
I intend to endeavour to follow the hon. member and deal with these matters in a dispassionate manner. As I listened to him concluding his remarks and making an appeal on behalf of freedom, I could not but agree when he referred to the difficulties Canada experiences by reason of being adjacent to a great nation to the south, with all its power and influence. I realized once more something of the challenge and the responsibility of maintaining in Canada that duality of culture to which he referred. I also accept and concur in the sentiments which he expressed.
Freedom is a subject that is always of interest. History shows that throughout the ages there has been a continuing contest between those who demand freedom of speech and those on the other hand who fear the use of that freedom. I am going to make some reference to freedom a little later on in connection with the C.B.C. I believe the time has come for a declaration additional to that made by the committee on a previous occasion in respect to that concept of freedom which is so much misunderstood today.
I want to make it clear, and as I said I am going to make reference to it later on, 68108-89
Committee on Broadcasting that in my opinion freedom in essence is the embodiment of the principle of the sacredness of the personality of the individual, and from that concept flows the idea of freedom of religion and of speech and of thought and association.
I think that periodically we have to make a declaration, each for himself, that freedom denies that we should be told what we are to read or hear or speak or write or think, except in so far as limitation of those rights is necessary in order to secure and assure the freedom of others. For if we ever come to the view that freedom consists in thinking what the majority believes or directs shall be thought, we shall have indeed defeated the concept for which democracy stands.
Hear, hear.

There is a tendency today-and it grows and attacks governments, and it attacks individuals as well-for people to believe that for which they stand is right, and that for which those opposed stand is wrong.
When I say these things I do not say that the use of freedom should permit or allow its abuse, for after all freedom consists in limiting the right of each of us in the interests of and the assurance to all of us of a like degree of freedom. If we ever arrive at a point-an unthinkable position-where each of us has to think what the majority demands, then we have indeed defeated democracy.
I believe that freedom can only exist where there is freedom of the mind, and that freedom can withstand wrong and evil only so long as it recognizes the right of each human being to find truth for himself. Democracy will not survive unless it depends for its living vitality on the persuasiveness of argument rather than uniformity of thinking determined directly or indirectly by the state. Freedom can only survive if each of us has freedom to inquire and to discuss; but freedom does not cover the right to speak disloyally, blasphemously or slanderously.
From time to time we have to do our thinking regarding freedom. A committee such as the radio committee is one that I am always proud to serve on, for in that committee there is a freedom from partisanship that too often bedevils some of the other committees set up by the house. There is freedom to think there, to disagree, to argue, and to discuss; and all of us within the same party do not have to have the same viewpoint regarding freedom. After all, freedom knows no bounds of party.

Committee on Broadcasting
I am one of those who fear for this nation if we ever arrive at a point when the governor or the board of governors of the C.B.C. are going to determine what I shall hear and when I shall hear it. I want to have the right to hear the exposition of views whether I agree with them or not. Providing that the delicacy of people is not shocked, or their religious sensibilities are not disturbed, I hope the day does not come in this nation when the C.B.C. will be in a position to determine for me what I shall hear over the air of this country. If we allow ourselves that luxury it will not be very long before the views expressed there will be the views *of the government of the day, and the opportunity for public opinion to be created by hearing all sides will have been denied. I say that by way of opening.
I listened to the minister today with great interest. He mentioned that I tried to trick him by a question, but that was farthest from my mind. I was trying to get information about what was going to happen and what was in the mind of the minister. He dealt with his stepchild with geniality, and throughout with pride. He pointed out that the C.B.C. has many friends; that he numbered himself among that host of friends; that it has much on the credit side of the ledger, and we all admit that. But, sir, changes have taken place within the last year or two that have also achieved a very unusual number of debits on the other side. I think one of the reasons for that is the fact, pointed out by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon with his usual comprehensiveness in discussing the matter, that now that the C.B.C. is freed from any direct responsibility to parliament to secure funds, it has also freed itself from doing some things that parliament has a right to demand that it shall do.
I believe criticism has been on the increase during the last year, and it is not criticism restricted to private radio stations, or to the press, or to chambers of commerce to which the minister referred. Criticism is becoming more general than ever before, and I think the reason is that there has been a tendency -and I speak wishing that I did not have to say the things that I am about to say- for the C.B.C. to become more absolute in its domination over private stations. It has revealed an attitude of mind in the promulgation of, or at least in threatening to promulgate, new rules, and also in allowing some of its programs to develop a sort of idolatrous adulation of some of the things this government does.
That is a trend, and unless we bring it before parliament it will continue. I am not going to single out any particular person


this evening in what I am saying. I believe that some recent broadcasts, and it has been particularly noticeable in the last six months, by some commentators bear all the evidence of an endeavour to build up the government and some of the ministers of the government in a manner that is detrimental to maintaining the non-political character of the C.B.C.
The news summaries by the C.B.C. are unbiased, as I see them. They are worth while, and they are listened to by the people of this nation. But some of the commentaries on the news by alleged independent commentators have shown that praise, however unjustified, of the government is not a disqualification of those who would make these commentaries and who do make them. The minister says there is no interference whatever by the government, and I will accept that statement. But there can be unconscious interference, which may be just as effective as conscious interference. I have noticed in the last year particularly that, with a number of exceptions, the commentaries on Sunday could not have been more effective as Liberal propaganda if the government had consciously intended that they should be such.
I believe in free speech, but freedom of speech does not consist in a national body or a national institution placing before the people, as unbiased commentaries, adulation amounting almost to idolatry, however commendable that may be to those in this country who enjoy power.
Constant criticism is another excess.
That is right. My hon. friend speaks with authority on that, and I agree with him entirely in that interruption. Now, returning once more to the regulations-
Hear, hear.

Today the regulations are out of date; they are obsolete. With few exceptions they go back to 1936, before the day of television. A little later on I am going to make a reference to television. I am all in favour of a Canadian national feeling. I am in favour of Canadian programs but, Mr. Speaker, the regulation that is about to be passed-if well-informed C.B.C. sources may be taken as correct in their assumption- that the Canadian content of programs must be increased by 48 per cent, indicates to me that the C.B.C., realizing that that cannot take place under present circumstances, is using its power against the tax-paying private station in a manner that is most unfair. How is a single station going to carry out a policy such as that?
Those are still matters for negotiation.

I appreciate that. I said it was in a period of suspended animation. But according to well-informed sources in the C.B.C., this is the regulation that is going into effect. However laudable the purpose may be of providing talent by edict, the result of this regulation, if carried into effect, will be unfair and unjust to the private stations of this country.
The minister says it is a matter of negotiation, and I agree. But I want to contribute my views at this moment so that, in so far as negotiation is concerned, my own views and those of many other Canadians on that subject will be known. I quote from the Vancouver Sun, which has never shown any particular desire to criticize this government. The editorial, appearing on October 31, 1952, read as follows:
C.B.C. thwarts talent
The eve of television development in Canada is a good time to expose the C.B.C.'s pretentious boast that it is the hothouse and forcing-bed of Canadian culture and entertainment talent.
It is just the reverse.
Then it goes on to say:
Private broadcasters say this situation effectively discourages the development of Canadian talent.
"There is no competition for talent," they point out, "since it must either work within the terms established by the C.B.C. at C.B.C.'s prices or have no field in nation-wide Canadian broadcasting."
That is the view generally held.
What paper was that?

That was the Vancouver Sun. I did not read all the editorial. It becomes more definite as it goes on, and uses some language that might not be regarded by the government as parliamentary. It does point out that a regulation such as that leads to other regulations, and such regulations will ultimately lead to the regimentation of private broadcasting stations in this country, if indeed the purpose of this regulation is not the achievement of that end.
Imagine what the newspapers in Canada would say if they were directed that they must publish editorials, 50 per cent of which dealt with Canadianism. How long would they stand regimentation such as that? When the C.B.C. was originally set up it was intended, in spite of what the government would assert today, that private stations could operate in co-operation with the C.B.C. In support of that statement I have the authoritative words of one of the first governors of this body. These regulations are not in effect yet, but my view is that they are dangerous in their potentialities. They would place the private stations in this 68108-891
Committee on Broadcasting country in the position of being pawns in the hands of the government competitors.
The minister endeavours to brush all this aside by saying the regulations are necessary. Certainly they are. Who argues against them? But regulations should be fair; they should be reasonable. If these regulations are brought into effect they will indeed provide an argument in support of those of us who believe that, as today there is a board of transport commissioners that determines disputes as between the government-owned railroad and the privately-owned railroad, so there should be a body similar in nature, if not the same body, in order to determine disputes as between the C.B.C. and the private stations. Last year the minister brought in legislation to provide for an appeal to the exchequer court.
That was in 1951.

Yes; in 1951. That was a sop. What is being asked for is not a right of appeal such as that, commendable and effective as it may be within its narrow compass. I say that a regulation such as the one I have been discussing is strong support of the need for a semi-judicial body to control the C.B.C. and to prevent injustice and unfairness from being perpetrated upon the private stations by the C.B.C. acting as both litigant and judge, a position that is a denial of every principle of right and justice.
I now pass on to a question that has been dealt with at considerable length today, namely that of television. I listened to the minister, and I tried to be impressed by his argument. In Saskatchewan we find that we are to be the forgotten province. There is nothing for us. We are not even worthy of a dam. But now, in addition to that, we are to receive no consideration in connection with television. Private companies everywhere are willing to establish television.
Where in Saskatchewan?
I do not know where in Saskatchewan.
No; you do not know.

I do not know that. If the minister is able to answer that question, I will be able to ask him a couple of questions. When I tried to get answers today he said the questions had tricky propensities about them.
He did not know; that is why he asked you.

As a matter of fact, the attitude of the government toward television has placed Canada farther back in television than any other nation similarly placed. I do

Committee on Broadcasting not understand this dog-in-the-manger attitude. If the government is not going ahead with television, why stop someone else from doing it?, My hon. friend says: Will anybody establish a station in Saskatchewan? Give them a chance. Will the minister now rise and say that if any private company is prepared to establish a television station in Saskatchewan, it will be allowed to do so?
Not that I know of.
I am asking whether they will be allowed to do so.
Not that he knows of, the minister says.

Mr. Speaker, as far as I
know no applications have been received from private individuals in the province of Saskatchewan. Should an application come from somebody in the province of Saskatchewan, it will be given consideration.
Oh, oh.

There is nothing to laugh at about it. The hon. member asked for an answer and I am giving it. Should an application come from somebody in the province of Saskatchewan, it will be given consideration by the Department of Transport and by the governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Pass the buck.
The operators are not laughing.

Television applications have been receiving that same kind of consideration for the last two years. Thirty-four of them have been held in abeyance, some of them for two years; yet my hon. friend says the same consideration will be given to any applicant in the province of Saskatchewan.
That will be 1965.
The hon. member will be gone by then.
So will the minister. Don't worry about that. Your whole party will be gone.
The hon. member will still be driving race horses.
No; they will still be on the payroll.
This government have only horses.
The minister will be able to ride one.
Don't you ever think it.
Mr. Speaker, these highly interesting interjections should be broadcast by the C.B.C.
The proceedings ought to be televised.

What I am trying to point out is this, subject to the assistance I am getting from both sides of the house. As television expands, radio recedes. Wherever television is allowed to establish itself, ordinary radio broadcasting in effect ceases.
Oh, no; that is not the experience.

Of course the minister speaks as an authority. I am just going to quote the former head of the National Broadcasting Company, Mr. Merlin H. Aylesworth. He said "Radio is doomed". A little later he said: "Radio is the only American industry that died in its infancy". He goes on to point out that when television finally is established, people cease to use the ordinary radio. What is our position today in Canada? We have promises for the future. The private broadcasting stations are placed in the position that they may establish places where the pickings are no good. That is, in effect, the policy.
The minister nods his head to that statement.

The minister agrees. I am glad to have his approval of what I have stated. In effect the position is this. The C.B.C. exercises a selectivity in examining all parts of the country; and having decided that some time in the future they may do something-and they do not yet know when they are going to start in various provinces -they say: This area looks profitable, so we are going to set it aside as an area in which we may establish, but until we decide, no one in that area shall have television. To me, Mr. Speaker, that is a denial of every right of private enterprise.
And of the Canadian people.

It is a denial of the right of the Canadian people to hear Canadian programs. Instead, they are being forced into the position mentioned by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) a moment ago, namely of being obliged to accept United States programs, to turn on their television sets to hear what the United States has to say rather than having a government or a broadcasting corporation that is prepared to go

ahead in Canada and assure Canadians of some of this Canadian unity of which we hear so much prated.

Ten o'clock.
On motion of Mr. Diefenbaker the debate was adjourned.
